title: The poet
hookLine: the poet sees and names what others feel (The Poet, 1844)

cards: A friend listens to you describe a bad week: the restlessness, the checking of the phone, the way your old street keeps coming to mind. Then they say one word. "Homesick."
Something clicks. That's it. The feeling didn't change, but now it has a handle, and you can pick it up and look at it.
Emerson put that kind of moment near the heart of the poet's work, in an essay called The Poet. Today, the one who names.

teach.b: First, Emerson's definition: "The poet is the sayer, the namer, and represents beauty." Not first a rhymer or a performer.

teach.h: EVERYONE FEELS IT; THE POET SAYS IT.
teach.b: The one who says what is there. Second, why we need a sayer at all. Emerson's point is that all people stand in need of expression.
Everyone has the raw experience: the sunset, the loss, the love, the dread. A person can feel it all and stay quiet, not from shallowness but because the words don't come.
The poet is the one in whom they come, and when they do, the rest of us recognize our own lives. That's why a good line of poetry can feel less like news and more like being found.
Third, a short phrase from the same essay: "Language is fossil poetry." Every ordinary word, Emerson says, was once a bright new picture someone made.
Over time it hardened and got buried in everyday talk, like a shell in stone. When you speak, you're using poems other people made, worn smooth. Fourth, what this means for anyone, poet or not.
Naming is a small act of poetry. Not bad, but lonely. Not angry, but embarrassed.
Not tired, but tired of being the only one who remembers.
When a feeling gets its exact name, it often loosens, and you can tell someone, or yourself. Emerson's poet does this for a whole people. Anyone can do it for one afternoon.

how: Readers of Emerson's The Poet often take it as a call to look for precise words for experience, and some keep journals or write poems for exactly that reason.

o: for Emerson, the sayer who finds words for what all feel
a performer who reads verses aloud to a crowd
anyone who writes lines that rhyme and keep a beat

games.q: inside Emerson's The Poet: tap the pairs.

s: Emerson defines the poet mainly as someone who rhymes
he calls the poet "the sayer, the namer."
every ordinary word was once someone's bright new picture.
in the essay, only poets have deep experiences
everyone has them; the poet is the one in whom the words come.

games.q: you're stuck in a mood you can't shake, and someone asks what's wrong. you've said "nothing" twice. what does Emerson's poet do?
o: wait for the mood to pass in silence.
look for the exact name of the feeling.
games.why: for Emerson the poet is "the sayer, the namer." a feeling with an exact name has a handle; you can pick it up and show it to someone.

practice: Notice what's here right now, under the surface, and give it a first rough word: fine, bad, off. Then ask, more exactly?
Try words gently, the way you'd try keys in a lock, restless, left out, hopeful but scared to say so, until one turns, and hold that name for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The poet. Emerson's sayer and namer, the one who finds the words for what others feel and can't say. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: name it. A feeling with a name is easier to carry. I'll be here tomorrow.
